items.title: Karnataka SIR: 43.8 lakh notices to be issued, Bengaluru accounts for 24 lakh
items.summary: The Karnataka Election Commission will issue notices to 43.8 lakh voters during the next phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Bengaluru accounts for more than half of recipients, with 24.05 lakh voters across its four electoral districts set to receive notices. Of these, 20.35 lakh voters have been flagged for “logical discrepancies” in their enumeration forms, while 23.45 lakh could not provide mapping details from the 2002 electoral roll. The notices will be issued after draft electoral rolls are published on August 24. The claims and objections period will continue until September 23, while their disposal will continue until October 22. The Chief Electoral Officer’s office has identified nine categories of logical discrepancies. These include implausible age gaps between parents and children, discrepancies in fathers’ names and differences between current and previous electoral records. Other categories include age gaps between siblings, unusually high numbers of children mapped to a parent, and discrepancies in voters’ own names between the current roll and the previous SIR. items.title: Ex-SC Judge from Telangana to head panel probing NEET protest police excesses
items.summary: The Supreme Court has formed a five-member High-Powered Enquiry Committee (HPEC) headed by former judge R Subhash Reddy to probe alleged police excesses during NEET protests. The order was issued on July 18 but made public only on Thursday, August 20. A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana directed the panel to examine allegations of police excesses, violence against protesters and counter-allegations of violence and vandalism by demonstrators during the protests. The committee will examine 12 issues, including the use of pellet guns, electric batons, lathicharge and tear gas, alleged violence and harassment of women protesters, surveillance of demonstrators, the use of prohibitory orders and the invocation of Section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. R Subhash Reddy, who will head the committee, served as a judge of the Andhra Pradesh High Court before his elevation to the Supreme Court in 2018. He was the first judge from Telangana to be elevated to the Supreme Court and retired in January 2022. Justice A Badharudeen passed the order on appeals filed by social activist M Geethanandan, Binu, Ramesan and Anilkumar, who were found guilty by a sessions court and sentenced to five years in jail over a violent confrontation between police and adivasi protesters at the Muthanga in 2003 The High Court had earlier observed that the trial court's finding on criminal conspiracy under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) was only prima facie in nature, and not conclusive. Justice A Badharudeen The Muthanga land struggle stemmed from an eviction drive carried out by the Kerala Police at the Muthanga Wildlife Sanctuary in Wayanad in 2003. The eviction drive led to a violent confrontation between the police and Adivasi protesters, which escalated into police firing. Five protesters and police constable KV Vinod died in the incident. items.summary: In a key judgment on recruitment of judicial officers, the Supreme Court on Friday upheld its May 2025 ruling that mandated law practice as a condition for entry into judicial service, but reduced the experience prescribed at the bar from 3 years to 1 year. Pertinently, the candidates who succeed at the judicial service exam will have to undergo one year of intensive training at the State Judicial Academy followed by six months’ clerkship under the District Judge/Higher Judicial Service and six months under a sitting High Court judge. The Court has granted a key exemption with regard to a transition period running up to March 31, 2027. For candidates applying within that date, no law practice experience would be required and they shall be deemed to have completed one-year law practice. items.title: When old statutes meet new codes: The conundrum with India’s Labour Codes and State-specific legislations
items.summary: The field of labour and employment in India has traditionally been vast and fragmented, governed by various legislations at the Central and State level. As a result, there has always existed a wide array of legislations which were required to be examined independently and cohesively, to identify the compliance requirements and the provisions that were applicable to employees. During the years 2019 and 2020, a progressive and revolutionary step was taken towards attempting to simplify the labour laws in the country by consolidating labour legislations into the four Labour Codes. While the Central government has brought the Labour Codes along with the Central Rules into force and effect, a majority of the states are still in the process of finalising and issuing the final State Rules to each Code. Among the four Codes, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, has become paramount in governing the working conditions of workers/ employees, specifically regulating the day-to-day aspects of employment, such as working hours, leave, etc., and this is being provided for under one specific statute. items.title: Should right to work be made fundamental right? Supreme Court on plea for minimum wage in rural employment schemes
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday questioned whether the statutory guarantee of employment for rural workers can be placed on the same footing as the fundamental right to life and dignity under Article 21 [Aruna Roy v. Union of India] . A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana noted that the Constitution does not recognise the right to work as a fundamental right. Instead, the Court observed, the Constitution places it among the State's obligations under the Directive Principles of State Policy. “The Constitution does not make the right to work a fundamental right. In fact, it is only a democratic aspiration under Part IV. To achieve that aspiration, the State formulates a policy where work is provided at a graded compensatory level. Should we create it on a par with Article 21?” said Justice Bagchi. He then flagged the broader constitutional implications of elevating the right to work to the level of an enforceable right, particularly if the State were to scale back its social welfare measures. “That is a very big question which we need to answer. items.title: Delhi HC rejects Khan Market Association's plea seeking uniform valuation method to determine property tax
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday rejected a plea by Khan Market Welfare Association seeking directions to the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) to adopt a uniform valuation method for calculating property tax in its jurisdiction [Khan Market Welfare Association v UOI & Ors] . NDMC area includes locations such as Connaught Place, Khan Market, Chanakyapuri and many other posh commercial and residential locations in Lutyens' Delhi. A Division Bench of Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain dismissed the plea, holding that the Court cannot issue directions on how a statutory authority like NDMC should formulate and administer the methodology for determination of rateable value (an official estimate of a property's annual open-market rental value). “The Court cannot, under the guise of issuing a mandamus, substitute its own formulation for that of the competent statutory authority. The principle is not that the exercise of statutory power is immune from judicial review, rather, it is that judicial review is directed towards the legality of the exercise of power and not towards the Court itself undertaking the function entrusted to the statutory authority,” the Court observed.
